title: Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Surgery in Immunocompromised Patients
summary: Immunocompromised status alone is not a blanket indication for broader-spectrum or prolonged surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis. Core principles remain: select an agent targeted to expected flora, dose/infuse correctly, and discontinue within 24 hours for most procedures. Limited, procedure-specific evidence suggests no routine benefit to extended or postoperative antibiotics, with potential harm from resistance and C. difficile. Individualize for neutropenia, transplant recipients, mucosal-breaching dental procedures, and the presence of prosthetic material.
clinicalQuestion: What is the evidence-based approach to perioperative antimicrobial prophylaxis in immunocompromised surgical patients?

heroStats.label: Prolonged prophylaxis appropriateness issues
heroStats.value: Up to 40% inappropriate prescriptions in audits [1]

heroStats.label: Dental procedures in chemo/transplant
heroStats.value: Randomized data support targeted prophylaxis when mucosa is breached [2]

heroStats.label: ICU prophylaxis practice
heroStats.value: Two-thirds of prophylaxis courses were SAP or for immunocompromised hosts in a single-center study [3]

keyMoments.title: Immunocompromised ≠ automatic broadening
keyMoments.body: Use standard, procedure-specific prophylaxis; broaden only for prior MDRO colonization, severe beta-lactam allergy, or local epidemiology. Overuse increases adverse events and resistance [1], [3].

keyMoments.title: Timing and duration are decisive
keyMoments.body: Administer within 60 minutes before incision (120 minutes for vancomycin/fluoroquinolones), redose by intraoperative half-life and blood loss, and stop within 24 hours in most cases; extended courses do not reduce SSIs and increase harms [1].

keyMoments.title: Procedure-specific evidence in immunocompromise is sparse
keyMoments.body: Dental procedures with mucosal trauma in chemotherapy or transplant patients show benefit from targeted prophylaxis in RCTs, but routine postoperative antibiotics after dermatologic surgery do not reduce infections despite immunosuppression [2], [4], [5].

keyMoments.title: ICU and drains: selective signals
keyMoments.body: Antibiotic prophylaxis for chest drain insertion in non-ICU settings reduces empyema (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.13–0.49) and pneumonia (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.24–0.71); extrapolation to immunocompromised ICU patients requires caution [3].

keyMoments.title: Stratify by type of immunosuppression
keyMoments.body: Neutropenia, solid organ or stem cell transplant, high-dose steroids, and biologics carry different risks. Align prophylaxis with expected flora for the surgery plus individualized risk factors rather than immunosuppression alone [6], [7].

sections.title: Stepwise Strategy for Perioperative Prophylaxis in Immunocompromised Hosts
sections.blurb: Apply standard surgical prophylaxis principles, then layer patient-specific risk adjustments supported by evidence.

steps.title: Define the immunocompromised state and risks
steps.body: Characterize neutropenia depth/duration, transplant status and time post-transplant, active chemotherapy, high-dose steroids or biologics, HIV with low CD4, and colonization with MDROs. This stratification informs whether deviations from standard prophylaxis are warranted [6], [8], [7].

steps.title: Choose procedure-specific agents
steps.body: Select narrow-spectrum agents covering expected flora (e.g., cefazolin for clean-contaminated general surgery). Reserve broader agents for specific indications (enteric contamination, biliary sepsis, prior ESBL/CRE colonization) rather than immunosuppression alone [1], [3].

steps.title: Optimize timing, dosing, and redosing
steps.body: Administer within the optimal window before incision, ensure weight-based dosing, and redose intraoperatively based on agent half-life and blood loss. These measures have the largest effect on SSI reduction across populations, including immunocompromised patients [1].

steps.title: Limit duration
steps.body: Discontinue within 24 hours for most operations; prolonged postoperative prophylaxis shows no benefit and increases adverse outcomes, including C. difficile and resistance, even in higher-risk hosts [1].

steps.title: Address special procedures and sites
steps.body: For dental procedures with mucosal trauma in chemotherapy or transplant recipients, targeted prophylaxis reduces bacteremia-related complications in RCT data [2]. In dermatologic surgery, routine postoperative antibiotics do not lower SSI rates despite immunosuppression status [4], [5]. Chest drains may benefit from prophylaxis in selected settings, though data derive from non-ICU cohorts [3].

sections.title: When to Modify Standard Prophylaxis
sections.blurb: Use this checklist to identify situations that justify deviating from standard surgical prophylaxis pathways.

cards.title: Escalate Spectrum
items: Documented colonization or recent infection with MRSA, ESBL, CRE, or VRE; add or substitute agents accordingly [1], [3]
Severe beta-lactam allergy; use vancomycin plus gram-negative coverage aligned to procedure [1]
Gross contamination or breach into infected fields (e.g., perforation); manage as treatment, not prophylaxis [1]

cards.title: Extend or Add Doses (Intraoperative)
items: Prolonged operations exceeding 2 half-lives of the agent; redose intraoperatively [1]
Excessive blood loss (>1500 mL); redose accordingly [1]

cards.title: Special Populations
items: Chemotherapy or transplant patients undergoing dental procedures with mucosal trauma: consider prophylaxis per RCT data [2]
Dermatologic surgery: do not use routine postoperative antibiotics despite immunosuppression; no benefit demonstrated [4], [5]
ICU patients with chest drain insertion: prophylaxis may reduce empyema/pneumonia in non-ICU data; individualize in immunocompromised ICU patients [3]

cards.title: De-escalation and Stewardship
items: Stop prophylaxis within 24 hours for most procedures; longer duration is rarely indicated [1]
Avoid substituting therapeutic regimens for prophylaxis without evidence of infection [1]
Monitor local SSI rates and resistance patterns; update pathways regularly [3]
